problem:
Express $z=\frac{4}{1+\text{i}\sqrt{3}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$ Give the **exact** values of $r$ and $\theta ,$ in **radians** from $[0,2\pi ).$

$z=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(${{field-2}}$)+i\operatorname{sin}⁡(${{field-3}}$))$

examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Quotient of Complex Numbers in Polar Form
examples.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\textrm{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\textrm{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $2+\textrm{i}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{3}{2-\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{3(2+\text{i})}{(2-\text{i})(2+\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{3(2+\text{i})}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}(2+\text{i}) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}+\frac{3}{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\textrm{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z| = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} .
$$

So, for $z= \dfrac{6}{5} +\dfrac{3}{5}\textrm{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{6}{5})}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{36+9}{25}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{45}{25}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta$  represents the argument $\arg(z).$ Since $x = \dfrac{6}{5}$ and $y = \dfrac{3}{5}$ are both positive, $z$ lies in the first quadrant. So, we can find $\theta$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{(\frac{3}{5})}{(\frac{6}{5})}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =0.464,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places. 

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z = \dfrac{3\sqrt{5}}{5} \left (\cos(0.464)+ \textrm{i} \sin(0.464) \right)
$$

feedback.problem:
Express $z=5-11\text{i}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$ Give the **exact** value of $r$ and round $\theta $ in **radians** from $[0,2\pi )$ to **two decimal places**.

$z=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(${{field-2}}$)+i\operatorname{sin}⁡(${{field-3}}$))$
feedback.worked_solution:
In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=5-11\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(-11)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+121} \\  & =\sqrt{146}.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=5$ is positive and $y=-11$ is negative, $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-11}{5}| \\  & =2\pi -arctan\,(\frac{11}{5}) \\  & ≈5.14,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places. 

Finally, we write the complex number $z=5-11\text{i}$ in polar form:

$$
z=\sqrt{146}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5.14)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5.14))
$$
